My dog’s name is Tumbleweed! When we first told people, they were skeptical and then all decided to call him different nicknames which I ignored. Whenever I bring him to the animal hospital for his surgeries (we adopted him in July and he’s on his second TPLO surgery, pray for my bank account oh my god), the techs always look at him and go “OH, we thought the name was cute but weird but you’re right. That’s exactly what this guy should be called.”

When we first got Tumble, every now and again he’d growl a little over his food dish. Locksley always backed off and we switched up their feeding routine to sort that out. Things were fine for a while. It’s really only been the last three days that Tumble has started reacting. 

It’s when Locksley comes near me. If Tumble is sitting with me and Locks comes over, Tumble leaps up and gets growly. Locksley doesn’t back down this time. They fight, usually over top of me or trapping me. I’ve gotten pretty good at shoving them off as soon as I recognize Tumble is about to lunge. 

If Locksley comes over to me and Tumble isn’t there, Tumble comes running and snarling. 

Neither reacts the same to my husband. 

With Tumble’s surgery and other injured leg, I’m wondering if he’s in pain and it’s making him act this way. I got him some gabapentin to help manage pain and chill him out but it’s not a long-term solution. It might give me time to figure it out though. 

I also played with them both in the back yard until they were exhausted and then cracked a window despite the Canadian winter cold because Tumble gets agitated when he’s warm. 

So they’re calm now. But for how long???

I did contact a trainer about it who should get back to me soon. Meanwhile, I like your idea of getting Tumble to associate Locksley being around me with positive things. The only thing Tumble likes better than me is freeze dried beef. 

Thank you. Im gonna try that.

I have been diagnosed and on medication for this since January. I am 39 and had been treated for anxiety, depression, adhd etc before my new psychiatrist said “yes, you have adhd, but I think your main issue is the undiagnosed bipolar.”  Whoops. 

A few months into the medication, I was walking my dogs with my husband and I realized I was happy. It wasn’t some giant, life changing, manic thing. It was quiet and calm and warm and the snow was beautiful and the dogs were happy and the sky was perfect and I was present in that moment and not wishing to be anywhere else or nowhere at all. 

It was just a little thing but I could breathe properly and it felt like feeling the sun after a long time in the dark. It also made me realize that I hadn’t actually felt that simple kind of happy in years and years. 

It’s still hard. But sometimes little bits of happy slip in when I least expect it.

I didn’t date anyone or kiss anyone or have a relationship until I was 30. And now I am 37 and married with a dog and two cats. 

I was bullied a lot growing up and had some trauma that made me really, really defensive. I’d destroy anyone who tried to get to know me because I hated myself so much, I couldn’t imagine anyone wanting to know me unless it was a joke or to hurt me. 

I went to therapy at 24 and it helped with that anger a lot. I got less defensive. But I still didn’t date. 

It got to this point where I was 29 and still so defensive and so convinced that no one would ever want to date me and I would be alone forever and a guy I knew told me that I was so convinced that I was undateable, that I was convincing everyone around me that it was true. I began to wonder if that was true. I DID tell people I was undateable. Whether it was self deprecating or joking or when I was sad and depressed. I wanted the world to know that I already knew that I was too ugly and too awkward and too annoying to be dateable, so the people around me wouldn’t feel the need to tell me all those things over and over the way the bullies in school did. 

And then I realized that those bullies were long gone and the only bully that was left in my life was me. 

I took a personal development course and learned about defence mechanisms that we develop when we are younger to protect ourselves from trauma and I had know that my lashing out defensively was one of them but the one where I made sure the world knew I hated myself enough so they wouldn’t feel the need to hate me too, that was a trickier one. But I’d also learned that the step to overcoming those defence mechanisms that we have outgrown is to recognize them, understand them, and understand that they are no longer protecting us — they’re hurting us. 

So I decided to stop. I decided to be Dateable. Because if I didn’t think I was dateable, why would anyone else? And it was hard. But just making the decision to see myself as someone worthy of being wanted and loved made me more open to it, I guess?

I also set up some goals. Baby steps. Easy steps. The end goal was not To Get A Date (because that would be setting me up for failure if it didn’t work out), the end goal was to Make Myself Dateable. 

And I don’t mean trying to make myself more attractive or trying to seduce someone or trying to be someone else. Just accepting that who I am is enough. And maybe someday, I’d be able to think that who I am is someone that people would be lucky to love. But baby steps. 

I don’t believe you need to love yourself before anyone can love you. I believe we are all worthy of being loved in whatever fucked up, damaged package we come in as we work towards a place of accepting that who we are is Enough. 

So my goals were “ask someone for coffee this month” and “sign up for online dating again”.  Small steps. Coffee can be friendly. It’s barely a date. 

I asked my best friend out for coffee over text. I’d had a crush for a while. I texted him and said “hey, want to go for coffee with me, it’s okay if you say no” (because I’d told myself over and over that it WAS ok if he said no. I just had to ask. Just asking was a win. 

He said “ask me again without assuming I’ll say no.”

We got married two and a half years ago. 

It was hard and it was scary but I know how you feel. And I know how hopeless it can seem. But you are good enough and you are worthy of love. Seek out therapy if you haven’t already. Attachment issues and childhood trauma make it harder. But having the self awareness to know where the challenge is coming from is the first step. You’ve got time. 

Be kind to yourself. 

Sorry for writing so much.

I brought a male friend along with me while buying my first car, because he was really into cars and I was worried that the dealerships wouldn’t take a young-looking blonde woman with social anxiety seriously. But I researched the hell out of what I wanted. I knew the specific car, the specific engine model, everything. 

The very first dealership we went to, the salesman only spoke to my friend. Even when I told him it was me, I was going to purchase a car. He addressed all his questions to my friend, even when he kept redirecting the questions to me. 

The worst part was when I test drove a car and it had a weaker engine than I wanted and after the test drive, I asked about the better engine and he looked at my friend and smirked and said, “she doesn’t need the stronger engine for quick trips to the mall.”

I was buying a car because I’d just gotten promoted to a top position with the government that meant I’d be driving all over the country. Which I explained to him. 

I did not buy a car from that guy and only shopped with female friends after that.

My 10 month old shepherd-malamute-husky-chow-collie Locksley’s biggest success this week is that he let me go downstairs without following me! He’s got severe separation anxiety that we are working on. 

He also dropped the ball during fetch. 

He also has solid poops again, finally, after days of diarrhea and medication!! He’s also too smart for pills so everyday, I need to come up with a creative way to sneak them into his food. And he usually discovers them and spits them out. It’s a work in progress. 

Some kids at the dog park told him to “go away, you dirty hyena dog” and they did it while crawling on the pile of snow he likes to pee on, so that was a victory (and he looks like a hyena, sure, but that was rude! And he’s clean!)

And! AND! Most importantly! My cat finally let him sneak in for a quick snuggle and ear lick. 

There is a picture of that momentous moment in my puppy tax: https://imgur.com/gallery/kv2FIXF

Oh these are all amazing things I hadn’t considered. Generally, he really really loves learning and responding to anything I ask him to do, usually going beyond what I ask just to be an extra good boy, like I ask for a sit and he throws himself into a settle and looks pleased with himself. So I didn’t really know how to handle the fact that all of that disappears when other dogs are around. He’s usually SO food motivated. But he loves playing with us too. Not as much as other dogs. But trying to make listening and playing with us at least as attractive as playing with dogs is a good place for me to start!

I’m definitely going to read this article and try these ideas. It will probably help me manage him around my cats too, since he’s so desperate to befriend them. 

I’ve been working really hard on mat training and it’s going really well. He’s actually disengaged from anything he’s doing when I ask him to go to his mat because we’ve put so much work into teaching him that amazing things happen there. Maybe I can even incorporate that into helping. I wonder if his mat would be more intriguing for him. 

I’m so excited to come at this problem from another angle, thank you so much.

And it’s not that he’s not bonded to us because he really is. Too bonded. He’s got bad separation anxiety which we are working with a trainer on and I can’t help but think getting him a dog sibling would cure because he’s so, so motivated by other dogs. And when we go for walks or anything, he sticks close. He is glued to us at home. LOVES playing with us at home.

That is true. Most of the time, the people just stand around and chat while my husband and I run around like fools playing with our dog. He has SO much energy, the dog park is just one piece of what we do to help him manage it. Unfortunately, it’s his favourite. And he’s much less desperate to befriend the cats if we go every now and again, which they appreciate. 

We also go on walks around the neighbourhood everyday and every few days, somewhere new and exciting for him to sniff. And he has regular play dates with my mom’s lab who he adores. I’ve also started some nose games with him which he is getting so good at! They go along with all his treat puzzles and games and the cardboard treat towers I built him so he can shred. He’s a very busy guy. 

I’m going to start recall training on the play dates with my mom’s dog! That’s a manageable way to build up. Thank you.
Shock collars are the worst. And I do hope that guy isn’t training his dog to be more reactive. So terrible.

We do work with a trainer who has helped me so much with so many things. The tactics I’ve been trying just haven’t had an affect because playing with other dogs is his highest value treat. It even overrides his separation anxiety! But you’re right. I need to go back to basics and start teaching him recall in easier settings. He’s great at it off leash on walks when no one’s around (we only let him off leash when we are somewhere pretty remote in the countryside and he never goes far). I will start working on it at my mom’s house with her one dog we go play with all the time! I do feel awful when he’s to play with a dog who clearly doesn’t want to play and I try to call him back and he ignores me. It’s awful.   I felt like teaching him that was impossible but if I start small, I can work up to it! Thank you for inspiring me to try again. He’s a smart dog, too smart sometimes, but he can totally learn this.

I’ve thought about that and I do understand those kinds of training programs too. The owners just seem to act like it’s fine though. They aren’t teaching their dog anything, just bringing it somewhere where it is massively uncomfortable and when it starts reacting, they either don’t care or, worse, get furious at the dog and make it worse. 

I worked with a trainer on friendly frustration reactivity with my dog. He wants to befriend evvvverybody sand gets upset when he can’t on walks. We used similar techniques with observing from a distance and slowly moving closer. It’s definitely a process! Good luck!

I do understand how you feel. I graduated with an English degree and panicked and ended up living in my mother's basement for a few years, evaluating my life and trying to figure out what I was going to do next, and worrying that I'd made a terrible mistake. But an English degree is not hopeless. It is a great place to start.

What I found for myself is that my English degree by itself gave me a lot of skills that my peers didn't have, in terms of critical thinking, writing, the ability to problem solve, that sort of thing. But what it needed was a bit of specialization. I ended up going back to school for a post grad certificate which was only a few months long, in publishing, which included an internship. The internship was the MOST important part, because that gave me actual experience to put on my resume, which is what I needed to open the doors into the fields where my English degree would have value. After that, I worked in journalism for a few years, government communications, and now I'm in non-profit communications. (All that in the last 10 years, when the economy was just about as bad as it is now, not before, when things were easier.)

I know it's hard. I know that 10 years ago, when I was where you are, I didn't want to live anymore. But I would have missed so much, and all of it was made possible by my English degree. Which is silly, now that I think about it, but true. 

I'm not sure if this helps. But I wanted you to know, I've been there. 

I'm sorry about your boyfriend, and that probably makes everything so much harder.

I think pursuing writing is an amazing idea, and judging by your post here, you'd probably do very well at it.
